sections.label: Reported abuse of security officers
sections.summary: From 2018 to 2020, about 150 abuse cases were reported yearly, and a survey found four in 10 security officers experienced abuse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: From 2018 to 2020, there was an average of about 150 reported cases of such abuse a year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: A survey of security officers conducted by the Union of Security Employees and the Singapore University of Social Sciences last year found that four in 10 security officers experienced some forms of abuse at their workplace.

sections.label: Bill amends PSIA offences
sections.summary: The Bill will amend the PSIA to create offences against common types of abuse faced by security officers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The Bill will amend the PSIA to create offences against common types of abuse faced by security officers.

sections.label: Removing security consultants licensing requirements
sections.summary: MHA will remove licensing requirements for security consultants, letting the industry oversee them, as SPF assessed low risk of abuse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Moving forward, MHA will remove licensing requirements for security consultants to allow the industry to oversee them, including through SCAP.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: SPF has assessed that the risk of security consultants abusing their position to commit security-related offences is low, as they do not supply the actual security systems or have access to premises for the installation and maintenance of security systems.

sections.label: Clause 4 removes licensing activities
sections.summary: Clause 4 amends the PSIA to remove the mentioned activities from requiring licensing.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 4 thus amends the PSIA to remove the mentioned activities from requiring licensing.

sections.label: Enhanced punishment and licensing removal
sections.summary: The measures are enhanced punishment for abuse of security officers and removal of licensing requirements for security consultants.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: First, enhanced punishment for abuse of security officers to better protect them and allow them to discharge their duties with peace of mind.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Second, removal of licensing requirements for security consultants.

sections.label: Survey on abuse of officers
sections.summary: 40% of security officers who took part in a survey last year indicated they suffered some form of abuse at work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: Yet, 40% of the security officers who took part in a survey last year indicated that they suffered some form of abuse in the course of their work.

sections.label: Penalties for abusing security officers
sections.summary: Abusing a security officer on duty carries a maximum fine of $5,000 to $10,000 or one to five years' imprisonment, or both, benefiting 50,000 officers once the Bill passes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: If you abuse, attack or cause hurt to a security officer while on duty, you will face a maximum fine of $5,000 to $10,000 or maximum imprisonment of one to five years, or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: Once the Bill is passed, 50,000 security officers will benefit.

sections.label: Security officers abusing their power
sections.summary: Under section 17(C)(3) of the Bill, the accused must prove on a balance of probabilities that their conduct was reasonable to avoid conviction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: At the same time, security officers also need to be aware of the consequences of abusing their power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: However, under section 17(C)(3) of this Bill, it is stated that the accused has to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the accused’s conduct was reasonable in order not to be convicted in Court.

sections.label: Protecting security officers from harassment
sections.summary: Stereotypes lead some people to taunt and bully security officers, so proposed amendments protecting them from harassment and abuse, with higher penalties, are welcome.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: These stereotypes embolden some people, leading them to think they can taunt and even bully our security officers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: So, the proposed amendments to protect our security officers from harassment and abuse, with penalties pegged higher than if they were committed against members of the public, are very much welcome.

sections.label: Accreditation without licensing teeth
sections.summary: Buyers can opt for higher or lower skills, but accreditation without required licensing may let standards diverge across security companies, especially with low barriers to entry.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: At the same time, in an industry that requires a range of services, buyers have the flexibility to opt for higher skills when they need to, while opting for lower-level skills or prices when they do not.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: However, industry accreditation, without the teeth of licensing, where security consultants are encouraged to get accredited but not required to be accredited, does open up the potential for standards to diverge across security companies, especially when the barriers to entry in the business are not high.

sections.label: Consistent industry standards
sections.summary: It asks how MHA will ensure standards are consistent across industry players and continue to rise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: First, how will MHA ensure that standards are consistent across players in the industry and ensure that these standards continue to go up?

sections.label: Audits on accreditation and practices
sections.summary: It asks whether there will be regular audits on company accreditation course contents and industry and company practices, and what role MHA or other bodies will play.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Lastly, will there be regular audits on company accreditation course contents as well as industry and company practices, and what will be the role of MHA or other industry associations and bodies?

sections.label: Support for security Bill
sections.summary: The speaker says Singapore faces new threats and needs a strong, trusted private security industry working with law enforcement, and supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, growing up in Singapore, our nation's security is something that is easy for us to take for granted, but there are new threats in the world today and the importance of our nation's security cannot be underestimated.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: We must have a strong, capable and trusted private security industry working hand in hand with our law enforcement agencies, who have the trust and respect of the public.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the questions above, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Negligent security officers criminal offence
sections.summary: The change made it a criminal offence for security officers to be potentially negligent on duty, with fines up to $2,000 or jail up to three months.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The change made it a criminal offence for security officers to be potentially negligent while on duty, such as to fall asleep or to not respond promptly to certain calls for assistance.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If convicted of such an offence, an officer could be fined up to $2,000 or jailed for up to three months, or both.

sections.label: New offences against security officers
sections.summary: Clause 3 introduces new offences criminalising obstruction and abuse of security officers, with punishments set between those for public officers and ordinary citizens.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The key change brought about by this Bill is in clause 3, which introduces various new offences to criminalise acts of obstruction and abuse of security officers while on duty.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As for the calibration of punishments, I note that the punishments in the proposed sections 17A and B are set somewhere between the punishments for similar conduct against public officers and that against ordinary citizens.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thus, for instance, the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to a security officer in the course of his duty will attract imprisonment of up to five years, between the maximum jail terms in the Penal Code for similar conduct against a public servant which attracts seven years and that against ordinary citizens which attracts three years.

sections.label: Public patience with security officers
sections.summary: Members of the public can play their part by exercising patience and remembering that officers are simply trying to do their jobs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Members of the public, too, can play their part by exercising patience and remembering that the officers are simply trying to do their jobs.

sections.label: Security officers facing abuse survey
sections.summary: In a survey released in March 2021, four out of 10 security officers had faced some form of abuse, a 10% increase from eight months earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In the survey released in March 2021, four out of 10 security officers had faced some form of abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: This is a 10% increase from an earlier survey just eight months ago.

sections.label: Mobile app for reporting cases
sections.summary: The speaker hopes this case is the exception rather than the norm, and a mobile application will be launched by the end of the year for officers to report cases quickly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: We can only hope that this case is the exception rather than the norm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: We will launch a mobile application by the end of this year for officers to report cases quickly.

sections.label: Threatening and abusing security officers
sections.summary: Proposed section 17C makes it illegal for an individual to threaten and abuse a security officer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: First, the proposed section 17C makes it illegal for an individual to threaten and abuse a security officer.

sections.label: Harsher punishments and public support
sections.summary: Harsher punishments let officers work without fear, but subtler abuse needs the public, service buyers and employers to stand up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Imposing harsher punishments on abusers of our security officers will ensure that our officers can carry out their duties without the fear of repercussions or reprisals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: However, there are subtler forms of abuse faced by our officers which are not captured by the law and probably cannot be done so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Therefore, we, as the public, must also stand up against such disrespect of security officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Service buyers and employers are entrusted with this role.

sections.label: Rest areas and Workcare Grant
sections.summary: MOM, NTUC and SNEF issued 2019 guidelines on rest areas for low-wage workers, and a $1 million Workcare Grant was announced in May 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Other support includes the joint guidelines announced by MOM, NTUC, SNEF in December 2019 on the provision of proper rest areas for low-wage workers like security officers, as well as a $1 million Workcare Grant announced in May 2021 to help facilities owners set up new or upgrade existing rest areas for outsourced cleaners and security guards.

sections.label: SUSS and USE abuse study
sections.summary: A SUSS and Union of Security Employees study found 40% of security officers experienced abuse, more frequently during the COVID-19 pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: A recent study conducted by SUSS and Union of Security Employees (USE) revealed that 40% of security officers have experienced some form of abuse, with incidences of abuse occurring more frequently during the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.label: Public service worker provision clarification
sections.summary: The amendments cover a public service worker under section 6(5) of the Protection from Harassment Act but not the Private Security Industry Bill, prompting a clarification request.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The amendments to the Bill have made a special provision which stated that an individual would be covered by section 6(5) of the Protection from Harassment Act but not the Private Security Industry Bill if he or she is also a public service worker.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: This could have implications for security officers who are hired directly by public service agencies, if the penalties under the Protection from Harassment Act and other existing legislation are different from those covered by the amendments to the Private Security Industry Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I would just like to seek for clarification as to why and how the Bill differentiates between the two groups of security officers who are essentially carrying out the same job functions and are facing similar levels of job risks?

sections.label: Mandated rest area standards and training incentives
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether minimum rest area standards could be mandated and whether incentives could support enhanced training and reskilling for security officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: For instance, instead of having guidelines on rest areas for security officers, can the Government consider mandating the minimum standards for rest areas in the same way that the Government has mandated minimum standards for foreign worker dormitories?

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Also, given that the security landscape is getting more complex due to the multi-dimensional safety and security threats that we now face, would the Government consider introducing incentives to support security companies to send their officers for enhanced training and reskilling to combat evolving threats of terrorism, managing safety and security in the post-COVID-19 world, and to familiarise themselves with artificial intelligence and other forms of security-surveillance technologies?

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The men and women hired to protect security for properties such as condominiums, shopping centres, commercial buildings, just to name a few, are facing increasing incidents of abuse from visitors, residents and tenants at the properties they are assigned to.

sections.label: Body cameras and offender penalties
sections.summary: A speaker suggests mandatory body cameras for private security officers and community service plus social education for offenders.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Police officers can warn and arrest offenders on the spot, but how about our security personnel?

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to suggest that MHA make it mandatory for all private security officers to be equipped with body cameras.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: (In English): I would also suggest that in addition to the fines and jail terms, offenders be made to serve community service and undergo mandatory social education programmes, where they learn to respect people from different income and social groups.

sections.label: Security officer abuse survey results
sections.summary: Surveys in 2020 found 30% then 40% of surveyed security officers faced some form of abuse at work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the first survey conducted between January and February 2020, 30% of the security officers surveyed had faced some form of abuse in their course of work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: When the survey was conducted again between September and November in the same year, 40% of the security officers surveyed had faced some form of abuse in their course of work.

sections.label: Bill's three new offences
sections.summary: The Bill introduces three new offences protecting security officers on duty, with penalties pegged higher than for offences against the public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With such uncalled-for behaviour towards our security officers, this Bill is timely as it introduces three new offences to protect security officers when they are executing their duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With the amendments to this Bill, these offences will carry penalties pegged higher than if they were committed against the members of the public.

sections.label: Technology reduces security officer numbers
sections.summary: Technology lets each security officer monitor more areas, so employers need fewer officers and are urged to share cost savings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Previously, we needed many security officers for a particular place or building.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But technology has improved the quality of security officers' jobs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As a result, employers do not need to hire so many security officers anymore because each security officer is now able to use technology to monitor even more areas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Employers can certainly save costs, and here, I implore these employers to share the cost savings with your security officers.

sections.label: Sponsoring union membership fees
sections.summary: Noting some lower-earning security officers struggle with membership fees, the speaker calls on employers to consider sponsoring them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We acknowledge there are some lower-earning security officers who may find it challenging to pay the membership fees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Hence, I call on employers to consider sponsoring the union membership fees for all their security officers.

sections.label: Survey on abuse of security officers
sections.summary: A survey of 1,002 security officers found two out of five experienced some form of abuse during their work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Indeed, a survey of 1,002 security officers between September and November 2020 found that two out of five security officers had experienced some form of abuse in the course of their work.

sections.label: Scope of officer duty offences
sections.summary: Asks what counts as execution and discharge of an officer's duty and whether new offences cover only section 13 functions or any reasonably connected functions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share what counts as the execution and discharge of an officer's duty?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Do these new offences apply only to functions outlined in section 13 of the Private Security Industry Act or do they apply to any functions reasonably connected to a security officer's work?

sections.label: Harassment defence clarification request
sections.summary: Asks the Minister to clarify why the defence applies to intentional harassment under section 17C but not under POHA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister clarify why this defence applies to intentional harassment under section 17C when it does not apply to intentional harassment under POHA?

sections.label: Security officer abuse statistics
sections.summary: States that nearly a third of security officers have experienced abuse on the job, a 30% surge over two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Nearly a third of security officers have experienced abuse on the job, a 30% surge over the past two years.

sections.label: Body camera recommendation for guards
sections.summary: Urges the Government to consider recommending or requiring security guards to wear a body camera.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Similar to the point made earlier by Member Joan Pereira, I urge the Government to consider recommending or requiring security guards to wear a body camera.

sections.label: Long hours and extra work
sections.summary: States many security officers work up to 12 hours a day for six days a week, and hopes the Bill makes extra work beyond agreed scope explicitly illegal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Beyond the abovementioned issues, many security officers have to work up to 12 hours a day for six days a week to alleviate a persistent manpower crunch.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The long hours and lack of rest time make the job unappealing, which only perpetuates the problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I hope the Bill will introduce regulations to make it explicitly illegal for security officers to be tasked with extra work beyond the agreed job scope.

sections.label: Criminal record and licensing
sections.summary: Asks the Ministry to clarify whether a criminal record automatically disqualifies one from working in the security industry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: They were willing to attend the necessary courses to obtain the relevant skills.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, because they have a criminal record, they have had difficulties obtaining a security officer licence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Can the Ministry clarify whether a criminal record automatically disqualifies one from working in the security industry?

sections.label: Criminal records and security hiring
sections.summary: The passage says writing someone off for a criminal record seems contrary to advocacy for second chances and the Yellow Ribbon initiative.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: While security is an industry that requires a high amount of integrity and trust, writing someone off for having a criminal record seems to run contrary to our advocacy for giving second chances and for the Yellow Ribbon initiative.

sections.label: Protection and training for security officers
sections.summary: The passage states security officers must have more protection and training, and haphazard designation of unrelated work must be prevented.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Our security officers must have more protection, more training and we must prevent haphazard designation of work that is unrelated to their job.

sections.label: Survey on abuse of security officers
sections.summary: A Union of Security Employees survey released in March found two in five security officers faced some form of abuse at work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The results of a survey conducted by the Union of Security Employees, which were released in March this year, found that two in five security officers were exposed to some form of abuse in their line of work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: While there have always been existing laws to protect all from harassment and abuse, no special provision has been given before this specifically for security officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: That being said, I would like to ask MHA what will be done to ensure that security officers and members of the public will be made aware of these amendments so that our security officers will know their rights and be able to better assert themselves while carrying out their duties.

sections.label: Technology and outcome-based contracting
sections.summary: A vehicle management system cut manpower by two while delivering similar outcomes, prompting a question on encouraging outcome-based contracting and technology.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: With the use of technology such as a vehicle management system at the entrance to the residential site, they were able to cut down the manpower needed by two while continuing to deliver similar outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: For example, illegal parking can be better managed through gantries, signages and CCTV with Video Analytics rather than a patrolling security officer who is tasked with requesting that errant drivers move their cars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Thus, I would like to ask MHA if there are any plans to encourage the adoption of outcome-based contracting and technology to help make our security officers' work safer and more effective.

sections.label: Abuse surge and proposed Act enhancements
sections.summary: A USE and SUSS joint survey found abuse cases against security employees surged by as much as one-third since the pandemic started.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: In a joint survey conducted by USE and the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), cases of abuse against security employees have surged by as much as one-third since the pandemic started.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: We must send a clear message that any abuse of security officers will not be tolerated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: I, therefore, fully support the proposed enhancements to the Act, which will introduce new offences to address common types of harassment and abuse faced by our security officers in the course of their duties.

sections.label: Security officers working 12-hour days
sections.summary: A TODAY newspaper report says many security officers work up to 12 hours a day, the labour law limit, due to insufficient manpower.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: According to a report by the TODAY newspaper, many security officers work up to 12 hours a day, which is the limit under our labour laws, due to insufficient manpower.

sections.label: MP appeals rejected security licences
sections.summary: An MP receives appeals from residents whose security officer licence applications were rejected by Police due to past convictions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: As a Member of Parliament, I sometimes receive appeals from residents whose application for a security officer's licence was rejected by the Police because they had a past conviction.

sections.label: Three new offences for security officers
sections.summary: Three new offences will be enacted to protect security officers while they are executing their duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, three new offences will be enacted to protect security officers while they are executing their duties.

sections.label: Sections 17A to 17C offences
sections.summary: New sections 17A to 17C will make it offences to assault, hurt or harass security officers whilst carrying out their duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The new sections 17A to 17C will make it offences to assault, hurt or harass security officers whilst they are carrying out their duties.

sections.label: Abuse frequency rose to 40%
sections.summary: Findings showed a third of security officers faced abuse last year, rising to 40% this year, attributed to their greater pandemic role.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Last year’s findings showed that a third of security officers faced abuse and this year’s findings found that the frequency had increased to 40%, with the increase being attributed to the greater role that security officers were required to undertake due to the pandemic measures.

sections.label: USE abuse-reporting app launch
sections.summary: The USE is rolling out an easy-to-use app for officers to report abuse and seek advice, to be launched by the end of the year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But as mentioned by several speakers earlier, the USE is rolling out an easy-to-use app, where officers can now report abuse that they have faced and they can seek advice on how they can proceed to commence the process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This app will be launched by the end of the year.

sections.label: SAS flags Savills tender clauses
sections.summary: SAS called out discriminatory and unfair clauses in a Savills tender for Hillview Heights, including immediate removal, race and age discrimination clauses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: SAS recently called out some of these discriminatory and unfair clauses in a tender document that was put out by managing agent Savills Property Management on behalf of its client, Hillview Heights condominium.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We identified three specific clauses of concern: an immediate removal clause allowing the managing agent to essentially, summarily dismiss security officers, a clause that appeared to discriminate on race and a clause that appeared to discriminate on age.

sections.label: Managing agents' absolute dismissal right
sections.summary: The passage states managing agents and buyers can require contractors to remove employees, with the right to dismiss being absolute, arbitrary and without due process, appeal or review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But the managing agents and buyers have been able to do this with impunity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I quote: "The MCST or its appointed Managing Agent shall be at liberty to require the Contractor to remove forthwith from the Estate any person employed by the Contractor who, in the opinion of the MCST or its appointed Managing Agent, has misconduct himself, or is incompetent and/or negligent in the performance of his duties, or whose employment is considered by the MCST or its appointed Managing Agent to be undesirable." As can be seen, Madam, the right to dismiss is absolute, it is arbitrary, with no due process or right of appeal or review.

sections.label: Proposed protections for outsourced workers
sections.summary: The speaker urges MOM to include measures preventing immediate removal demands, requiring written reasons, providing appeal and review, and proscribing discriminatory stipulations in service contracts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, I urge that MOM includes in the new legislation measures that prevent managing agents and buyers from demanding the immediate removal of outsourced workers at site; that if they do request a change, that they are required to provide reasons in writing and that there should be a mechanism for appeal and review against such requests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Of course, discriminatory stipulations in service contracts like those on age, gender and race should also be proscribed by the new law and should not be allowed in outsourced services tender documents and service contracts.

sections.label: Security consultant accreditation and self-regulation
sections.summary: The passage states a July examination had a one-third failure rate, 10 applicants for December 2021, 50 to 70 consultants expected accredited by end of next year, and removal from statutory licensing towards self-regulation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the first examination that was held in July, we had a one-third failure rate, so the bar is set very high, and intentionally so, because we only want truly competent and qualified persons to be accredited.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There are 10 persons who have applied as of today for the next examination scheduled in December 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And we expect to have accredited around 50 to 70 consultants by the end of next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Most importantly, the removal of security consultants from a statutory licensing regime in favour of an industry-led initiative is an important move towards self-regulation for this particular profession.

sections.label: Aspiration for workers' respect and dignity
sections.summary: The speaker recalls urging priority for a working environment affording workers respect and dignity, and says the amendments will go a long way towards that aspiration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In my maiden speech earlier this year, I urged that we make it a priority to ensure that all our workers have a working environment that affords them respect and dignity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I urged that we take steps to make sure that we take care of those who take care of us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The amendments introduced today will go a long way to bring us towards that aspiration.

sections.label: Greater protection and harsher penalties
sections.summary: The Bill offers greater protection and harsher penalties to those who cause harm to them, whether physically or not.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The Bill offers them greater protection and harsher penalties to those who cause harm to them, be it physically or not.

sections.label: Abuse and harassment cases against security officers
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister of State for an overview of abuse and harassment cases reported against security officers over the past three years.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: First, can the Minister of State give us an overview of the number of abuse and harassment cases reported against security officers by themselves, members of the public or security agencies over the past three years?

sections.label: Reporting channel for security officers
sections.summary: A Member asks if there will be a protocol, such as a whistle-blowing channel, for security officers to report abuse or harassment.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: With that, I would like to ask the Minister of State if there will be a proper protocol, perhaps a whistle-blowing channel, for security officers to use to report incidents of abuse or harassment?

sections.label: Working hour limits for officers
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the Ministry will limit officers' working hours, including mandated off days or off hours, without affecting their salary.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Will the Ministry introduce any limit to working hours, including mandated off days or off hours, for officers, without affecting their salary?

sections.label: Abuse cases and action taken
sections.summary: About 150 abuse cases per year occurred while security officers were on duty in the last three years, with action ranging from warnings to prosecutions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: As mentioned in my earlier speech, in the last three years, there was an average of about 150 cases of abuse while security officers were on duty per year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Depending on the facts and circumstances of each case, the action taken against offenders may range from stern warnings to Court prosecutions.

sections.label: Abuse of off-duty officers
sections.summary: Abuse of an off-duty officer related to execution of duties under section 13 of the PSIA may constitute an offence under new section 17C PSIA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: If a security officer is abused while off duty, but the abuse is in relation to the execution of the officer’s duties under section 13 of the PSIA, then an offence under the new section 17C PSIA may be made out.

sections.label: Security officers as Public Service Workers
sections.summary: Some security officers, such as those at public healthcare, step-down care or educational institutions, are already Public Service Workers under POHA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: To clarify, some security officers are already considered Public Service Workers under POHA, such as those deployed at public healthcare institutions, step-down care institutions or educational institutions.

sections.label: Security officer licence application appeals
sections.summary: Between 2017 and 2021, Police received an average of 300 security officer licence application appeals yearly, including from ex-offenders, about a fifth successful.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Between 2017 and 2021, the Police received an average of 300 security officer licence application appeals per year, including from ex-offenders, of which about a fifth were successful.

sections.label: Police approved body-worn camera requests
sections.summary: Between 2019 and 2021, the Police approved 43 requests from 15 licensed security agencies to use body-worn cameras at deployment sites.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Between 2019 and 2021, the Police approved 43 requests made by 15 licensed security agencies for the use of body-worn cameras at various deployment sites for their security officers.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Model security officer wages
sections.summary: The Progressive Wage Model has improved wages for about 40,000 security officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: For example, on wages, the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) has improved wages for about 40,000 security officers.

sections.label: Security officer overtime hours capped
sections.summary: Previously exempted security officers could work up to 95 overtime hours monthly, now capped at 72 hours monthly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Previously, with the exemption, security officers could work up to 95 hours of overtime per month and now, overtime is capped at 72 hours per month.

sections.label: Mobile app and misconduct complaints
sections.summary: A new mobile application by USE is coming, and no new unit is needed now to manage misconduct complaints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: And soon, as also mentioned by Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Thomas and Mr Abdul Samad, through a new mobile application by USE.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: There is no need to set up a new unit under the Police Licensing and Regulatory Department to manage complaints on misconduct of security officers, as suggested by Mr Ang, at this moment.

sections.label: Removing security consultancy from regulation
sections.summary: Persons providing only security consultancy services are removed from PSIA regulation, while other Section 18 services still require licensing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: To clarify, we are removing persons who only provide security consultancy services from regulation under the PSIA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
sentences.text: Persons who provide any other services that fall under Section 18 of the PSIA would still have to be licensed.
